analysis.answer: Current law allows adults 21 or older to possess up to one ounce of cannabis without penalty. The measure makes possessing any amount a misdemeanor punishable by up to 90 days in jail.

Direct costs include increased expenses for policing, prosecution, court administration, public defense, and jail operations. Opportunity costs include law enforcement resources diverted from other issues, as well as the lost income and employment prospects for individuals who acquire criminal records or spend time in jail.
Taxpayers bear the cost of the increased criminal justice enforcement. Individuals who possess cannabis bear the criminal penalties and associated personal and economic costs.
Some individuals may stop possessing or using cannabis, while others will likely continue but take greater measures to conceal it.
The measure addresses the perceived negative health or social effects of cannabis use by criminalizing its possession. The mechanism directly targets users with the threat of jail time.
Police and prosecutors gain power and discretion over arrests and charging decisions for cannabis possession.
Researchers disagree on whether criminalizing drug possession effectively deters use and improves public health, or whether it primarily increases social harm, stigma, and criminal justice costs.
Substantial resources will be absorbed by the criminal justice system to process arrests, prosecutions, and jail sentences for a newly created misdemeanor.
